papers.name: Paper 1 Thematic study and historic environment

topics.name: Option 10 Thematic study: Crime and punishment in Britain, c1000–present
points: c1000–c1500 Nature and changing definitions of crime: crimes against person, property and authority; Norman Forest Laws
c1000–c1500 Law enforcement and punishment: tithings, hue and cry, parish constable; Wergild, fines, corporal and capital punishment
c1000–c1500 Case study: influence of the Church; sanctuary, benefit of clergy, trial by ordeal
c1500–c1700 Nature and changing definitions of crime: heresy and treason; vagabondage and witchcraft
c1500–c1700 Law enforcement and punishment: town watchmen; corporal and capital punishment; transportation; the Bloody Code
c1500–c1700 Case studies: the Gunpowder Plotters 1605; Matthew Hopkins and the witch-hunts 1645–47
c1700–c1900 Nature and changing definitions of crime: highway robbery, poaching, smuggling; end of witchcraft prosecutions; Tolpuddle Martyrs
c1700–c1900 Law enforcement and punishment: Fielding brothers, police forces, end of public execution, prison reform (Howard, Fry)
c1700–c1900 Case studies: Pentonville prison; Robert Peel and the Metropolitan Police
c1900–present Nature and changing definitions of crime: new forms of theft and smuggling; driving, race and drug crimes
c1900–present Law enforcement and punishment: police specialisation and science, Neighbourhood Watch, abolition of the death penalty, open prisons, non-custodial sentences
c1900–present Case studies: conscientious objectors in the World Wars; the Derek Bentley case

topics.name: Option 10 Historic environment: Whitechapel, c1870–c1900: crime, policing and the inner city
points: Local context of Whitechapel: housing, overcrowding, Peabody Estate, workhouses; links between environment, poverty and crime
The inhabitants of Whitechapel: unemployment, lodging houses and pubs; Irish, Eastern European and Jewish migration
Organisation of policing in Whitechapel: the beat constable, H Division; alcohol, prostitution, gangs, anti-Jewish attacks
Investigative policing: detective techniques, Jack the Ripper and the media, Whitechapel Vigilance Committee
National and regional context: Metropolitan Police, CID, Home Secretary, Sir Charles Warren, public attitudes
Sources for the enquiry: local sources (census, Booth's survey, workhouse and police records) and national sources (newspapers, Old Bailey, Punch)
Source skills: strengths and weaknesses of sources, framing questions and selecting sources for an enquiry

topics.name: Option 11 Thematic study: Medicine in Britain, c1250–present
points: c1250–c1500 Ideas about the cause of disease: supernatural, religious and rational explanations; four humours, miasma, Galen
c1250–c1500 Approaches to prevention and treatment: bloodletting, purging; medical training and care
c1250–c1500 Case study: dealing with the Black Death 1348–49
c1500–c1700 Ideas about the cause of disease: continuity and change; Sydenham, printing, the Royal Society
c1500–c1700 Prevention, treatment and care: medical training; influence of Vesalius in England
c1500–c1700 Case studies: Harvey and the circulation of the blood; the Great Plague in London 1665
c1700–c1900 Ideas about the cause of disease: Pasteur's germ theory and Koch's work on microbes
c1700–c1900 Care and treatment: hospitals and Nightingale; anaesthetics and antiseptics; vaccination and the Public Health Act 1875
c1700–c1900 Case studies: Jenner and vaccination; cholera in London 1854, John Snow and the Broad Street pump
c1900–present Ideas about the cause of disease: genetic and lifestyle factors; improved diagnosis (blood tests, scans, monitors)
c1900–present Care and treatment: the NHS, antibiotics, high-tech treatments, mass vaccination, lifestyle campaigns
c1900–present Case studies: Fleming, Florey and Chain and penicillin; the fight against lung cancer

topics.name: Option 11 Historic environment: The British sector of the Western Front, 1914–18: injuries, treatment and the trenches
points: Context of the British sector: Flanders and northern France, the trench system, problems of terrain
Conditions and injuries: trench illnesses, rifle and explosive wounds, shrapnel, infection, head injuries, gas
The work of the RAMC and FANY: the chain of evacuation; the underground hospital at Arras
Medical and surgical developments: Thomas splint, mobile X-rays, blood transfusion and the Cambrai blood bank
Context of early 20th-century medicine: infection, aseptic surgery, X-rays, blood transfusion
Sources for the enquiry: national sources (army records, government reports) and local sources (personal accounts, hospital records)
Source skills: strengths and weaknesses of sources, framing questions and selecting sources for an enquiry

topics.name: Option 12 Thematic study: Warfare and British society, c1250–present
points: c1250–c1500 Nature of warfare: army composition, weapons, formations, decline of the mounted knight
c1250–c1500 Experience of war: feudal recruitment and training; impact of war on civilians
c1250–c1500 Case studies: the Battle of Falkirk 1298; the Battle of Agincourt 1415
c1500–c1700 Nature of warfare: changing army composition, muskets and pistols, a standing army
c1500–c1700 Experience of war: recruitment and training including the New Model Army; impact on civilians
c1500–c1700 Case study: the Battle of Naseby 1645
c1700–c1900 Nature of warfare: army changes, weapons and impact of industrialisation
c1700–c1900 Experience of war: Cardwell's reforms; civilians; press and photography in the Crimean and Boer Wars
c1700–c1900 Case studies: the Battle of Waterloo 1815; the Charge of the Light Brigade at Balaclava 1854
c1900–present Nature of warfare: modern weapons, transport and surveillance, guerrilla warfare
c1900–present Experience of war: conscription, the Home Front, conscientious objectors, censorship and propaganda
c1900–present Case studies: the Battle of the Somme 1916; the Iraq War 2003

topics.name: Option 12 Historic environment: London and the Second World War, 1939–45
points: Context of London in the war: centre of government, port and industry, preparations in 1939
Nature of attacks on London: East End docks, Black Saturday, V2 attack on Deptford, types of bomb
Impact of the Blitz on civilians: shelters, school and Bethnal Green disasters, disruption to daily life
London's response: the Royal Family, Cabinet War Rooms, Dig for Victory and public spaces
Context of the Blitz: its nature and purpose; propaganda and censorship
Sources for the enquiry: local sources (personal accounts, council records) and national sources (Mass Observation, newsreels, government records)
Source skills: strengths and weaknesses of sources, framing questions and selecting sources for an enquiry

topics.name: Option 13 Thematic study: Migrants in Britain, c800–present
points: c800–c1500 Context for migration: Vikings, Normans, Jewish traders; English economic and political context
c800–c1500 Experience and impact: legal status, relations with locals, Black Death, impact on culture and trade
c800–c1500 Case study: Viking York
c1500–c1700 Context for migration: migrants from Europe and Africa; trade, cloth industry, Protestant England
c1500–c1700 Experience and impact: relations with authorities and residents; impact on culture, industry and farming
c1500–c1700 Case studies: Flemish and Walloon migrants in Sandwich and Canterbury; Huguenots in 17th-century England
c1700–c1900 Context for migration: Ireland, Europe and the Empire; industrialisation, urbanisation, slavery
c1700–c1900 Experience and impact: relations with residents, the media, impact on industry, politics and cities
c1700–c1900 Case studies: Liverpool and Irish migrants; Jewish migrants in the late 19th-century East End
c1900–present Context for migration: Ireland, Europe, Empire and Commonwealth, refugees; decolonisation, EU membership, immigration law
c1900–present Experience and impact: anti-immigration and equal rights movements, Race Relations Act 1965, the media
c1900–present Case studies: mid-20th-century Bristol; Asian migrants in Leicester from 1945

topics.name: Option 13 Historic environment: Notting Hill, c1948–c1970
points: Local context: Caribbean migration, housing problems, slum landlords, Notting Hill Housing Trust, Portobello Road
Caribbean cultural influence: shops, cafés, shebeens, nightclubs, All Saints Road, 'pardner' schemes
Racism and policing: the 1958 riots, murder of Kelso Cochrane, Mosley's campaigns
Black activism: Claudia Jones, West Indian Gazette, origins of Carnival, the Mangrove and the Mangrove Nine
National context: post-war labour demand, Commonwealth links, the Swinging Sixties, poverty and policing in London
Sources for the enquiry: local sources (Caribbean community publications, council and police records) and national sources (census, polls, TV)
Source skills: strengths and weaknesses of sources, framing questions and selecting sources for an enquiry

papers.name: Paper 2 Period study and British depth study

topics.name: Period study P1 Spain and the 'New World', c1490–c1555
points: 1.1 Spanish exploration: Spain's crusading ambitions, Isabella's sponsorship, Columbus's 1492 voyage
1.2 Columbus reaches the Americas: Caribbean exploration, gold, relations with indigenous peoples, Treaty of Tordesillas
1.3 Spanish claims in the Caribbean: Santo Domingo, treatment of indigenous peoples, disease, slavery
2.1 The start of an empire: Balboa, Cuba, Magellan's voyage
2.2 The conquest of Mexico: Cortés, Montezuma, Tlaxcalan alliance, fall of Tenochtitlan
2.3 The impact of Spain in the Americas: Cortés as Governor 1523–28, consequences for the Aztecs
3.1 Pizarro and the conquest of the Incas: Cajamarca, the Inca revolt, siege of Cuzco
3.2 Expansion of the Spanish empire: viceroys, encomiendas, Las Casas, the New Laws 1542, silver
3.3 The impact of the 'New World' on Spain: bullion, the slave trade, government institutions

topics.name: Period study P2 British America, 1713–83: empire and revolution
points: 1.1 Developments in colonial society: expansion, social tensions, the tobacco trade, suppression of piracy
1.2 Slavery in North America: the Atlantic triangle, plantations, effects on colonial society
1.3 Problems within the colonies: Stono Rebellion, the New York Conspiracy, smuggling
2.1 Cultural developments: the Great Awakening, the Enlightenment, Benjamin Franklin
2.2 War in the colonies: King George's War, the French and Indian War, treaties of 1763
2.3 Aftermath of the French and Indian War: opposition to the Sugar Act, Pontiac's Rebellion
3.1 Growing opposition 1765–75: Stamp Act, Boston Massacre, Boston Tea Party, Continental Congresses
3.2 The War of Independence: Paine, the Declaration of Independence, Saratoga, Yorktown, Peace of Paris
3.3 Consequences of the war: slavery, indigenous peoples, resettlement of Loyalists

topics.name: Period study P3 The American West, c1835–c1895
points: 1.1 The Plains Indians: social structure, way of life, beliefs about land and war
1.2 Migration and early settlement: Oregon Trail, Manifest Destiny, Mormons, California Gold Rush
1.3 Conflict and tension: Permanent Indian Frontier, Fort Laramie Treaty 1851, early lawlessness
2.1 Development of settlement: transcontinental railroad, Homestead Act, Timber Culture Act, law and order
2.2 Ranching and the cattle industry: Abilene, the cowboy, ranchers and homesteaders
2.3 Changes in the way of life of the Plains Indians: Sand Creek, Red Cloud's War, Fort Laramie Treaty 1868
3.1 Changes in farming, the cattle industry and settlement: new technology, winter 1886–87, Oklahoma Land Rush
3.2 Conflict and tension: lawmen, range wars, Little Big Horn, Wounded Knee
3.3 Destruction of the Plains Indians' way of life: extermination of the buffalo, reservations, Dawes Act

topics.name: Period study P4 Superpower relations and the Cold War, 1941–91
points: 1.1 Early tension between East and West: the Grand Alliance, Tehran, Yalta and Potsdam, ideology, the atomic bomb
1.2 The development of the Cold War: Truman Doctrine, Marshall Plan, Berlin Crisis, NATO
1.3 The Cold War intensifies: the arms race, the Warsaw Pact, the Hungarian Uprising 1956
2.1 Increased tension: Berlin ultimatum, Cuban Revolution, Bay of Pigs, Prague Spring
2.2 Cold War crises: the Berlin Wall, the Cuban Missile Crisis, the Brezhnev Doctrine
2.3 Reaction to crisis: Kennedy in West Berlin, the hotline, arms control treaties
3.1 Attempts to reduce tension: détente, SALT 1, Helsinki Accords, SALT 2
3.2 Flashpoints: Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, Carter Doctrine, Olympic boycotts, Reagan and SDI
3.3 The collapse of Soviet control of Eastern Europe: Gorbachev's new thinking, fall of the Berlin Wall, end of the Warsaw Pact

topics.name: Period study P5 Conflict in the Middle East, 1945–95
points: 1.1 The British withdrawal from Palestine: King David Hotel bombing, UN Resolution 181, the 1948–49 war
1.2 Aftermath of the 1948–49 war: territorial change, Palestinian refugees, the IDF, US aid
1.3 Increased tension 1955–63: Nasser, attacks from Gaza and Sinai, the Suez Crisis
2.1 The Six Day War 1967: tensions with Syria and Jordan, superpower involvement, key events
2.2 Aftermath of the 1967 war: UN Resolution 242, occupied territories, terrorism, PLO expelled from Jordan
2.3 Israel and Egypt 1967–73: the Yom Kippur War
3.1 Diplomatic negotiations: the oil crisis, shuttle diplomacy, Camp David
3.2 The Palestinian issue: Arafat at the UN 1974, the PLO in Lebanon, the First Intifada
3.3 Attempts at a solution: Arafat's renunciation of terrorism, the Gulf War, the Oslo Accords

topics.name: British depth study B1 Anglo-Saxon and Norman England, c1060–88
points: 1.1 Anglo-Saxon society: monarchy, earldoms, local government, law, economy and the Church
1.2 The last years of Edward the Confessor and the succession crisis: the Godwins, Harold's embassy to Normandy, Tostig
1.3 The rival claimants for the throne: William, Harald Hardrada, Edgar; Gate Fulford and Stamford Bridge
1.4 The Norman invasion: the Battle of Hastings and reasons for William's victory
2.1 Establishing control: submission of the earls, rewards for followers, Marcher earldoms, castles
2.2 The causes and outcomes of Anglo-Saxon resistance 1068–71: Edwin and Morcar, northern revolts, Hereward at Ely
2.3 The legacy of resistance to 1087: the Harrying of the North, changes in landownership
2.4 Revolt of the Earls 1075: reasons, features, defeat and effects
3.1 The feudal system and the Church: tenants-in-chief, knights, Stigand, Lanfranc, Church reform
3.2 Norman government: centralised power, regents, sheriffs, forest law, the Domesday Book
3.3 The Norman aristocracy: culture and language; the career of Bishop Odo
3.4 William I and his sons: Robert's revolt, William's death, William Rufus defeats Robert and Odo

topics.name: British depth study B2 The reigns of King Richard I and King John, 1189–1216
points: 1.1 The feudal system: hierarchy, landholding, homage, knight service, forfeiture; role of the Church
1.2 Kingship and succession: Richard's and John's claims, characters and power; the murder of Arthur
1.3 Royal government and finances: rule during the king's absence, sheriffs, scutage, taxes of 1207
1.4 English society: towns and countryside, legal status of Jews, moneylending, pogroms 1189–90
2.1 The nature of crusading: crusading ideas, English attitudes, the English army
2.2 Richard and the Third Crusade: quarrel with Philip II, Acre, Arsuf, failure to take Jerusalem
2.3 The aftermath of the crusade: Richard's capture and the burden of the ransom
2.4 Richard, John and the loss of Normandy: Chateau Gaillard, loss of Normandy 1204
3.1 King John's dispute with the Papacy: causes, the Interdict, reconciliation with Innocent III
3.2 Worsening relations with the barons: taxes, fines, arbitrary rule, 1212 plot, 1214 defeat, 1215 rebellion
3.3 Magna Carta and the First Barons' War: Runnymede, main provisions, Rochester, Prince Louis
3.4 England in 1216: the succession problem, William Marshal as Protector

topics.name: British depth study B3 Henry VIII and his ministers, 1509–40
points: 1.1 Henry VIII, Renaissance Prince: England in 1509, Henry's character and style of government
1.2 The rise of Wolsey and his policies: reasons for his rise, wealth, reforms, the Amicable Grant
1.3 Wolsey's foreign policy: France and the Empire, Treaty of London, Field of the Cloth of Gold
1.4 Wolsey, the king's 'great matter' and his fall: annulment attempts, Clement VII, Wolsey's downfall
2.1 The rise of Cromwell 1529–34: early career, handling of the annulment, role as Chief Minister
2.2 Cromwell and the king's marriages: fall of Anne Boleyn, Jane Seymour, Anne of Cleves
2.3 Cromwell and government 1534–40: reform of government and finance, management of Parliament
2.4 The fall of Cromwell: Norfolk's influence, the Cleves marriage, execution 1540
3.1 The break with Rome: the campaign of 1529–33, Acts of Succession and Supremacy, enforcement
3.2 Opposition to, and impact of, the Reformation: Elizabeth Barton, Fisher, More, Cranmer's reforms
3.3 The dissolution of the monasteries: the 1535 commissions, winners and losers
3.4 The Pilgrimage of Grace 1536: reasons, Lincolnshire and Yorkshire risings, Aske and Norfolk

topics.name: British depth study B4 Early Elizabethan England, 1558–88
points: 1.1 The situation on Elizabeth's accession: society and government, legitimacy, gender, marriage, character, challenges
1.2 The 'settlement' of religion 1559: features, impact, role of the Church of England
1.3 Challenges to the religious settlement: Puritans, Catholics, the nobility, the Papacy, foreign powers
1.4 The problem of Mary, Queen of Scots: her claim; relations with Elizabeth 1568–69
2.1 Plots and revolts at home: Revolt of the Northern Earls, Ridolfi, Throckmorton and Babington plots, Walsingham, Mary's execution
2.2 Relations with Spain: commercial and religious rivalry, privateering, Drake
2.3 Outbreak of war with Spain 1585–88: the Netherlands, Robert Dudley, Drake's raid on Cadiz
2.4 The Armada: Spanish plans, key events, reasons for English victory
3.1 Education and leisure: education in the home and schools, sport, pastimes, the theatre
3.2 The problem of the poor: reasons for poverty and vagabondage, changing attitudes and policies
3.3 Exploration and voyages of discovery: new technology, trade, Drake's circumnavigation
3.4 Raleigh and Virginia: reasons for colonisation, Raleigh's role, failure of the first settlement

topics.name: Option 30 Russia and the Soviet Union, 1917–41
points: 1.1 Growing opposition to the Tsar: peasant and worker discontent, wartime defeats
1.2 The February Revolution: strikes in Petrograd, army mutiny, the Tsar's abdication
1.3 The Provisional Government: Dual Power, Order No. 1, Kerensky, the Kornilov Revolt
1.4 The Bolshevik Revolution: Lenin's April Theses, the July Days, seizure of power in October
2.1 Early consolidation 1917–18: decrees, the Constituent Assembly, Treaty of Brest-Litovsk
2.2 The Civil War 1918–21: causes, key events, reasons for Bolshevik victory
2.3 Moves towards totalitarianism: Red Terror, the Cheka, Kronstadt, centralisation
2.4 Economic and social change 1918–24: War Communism, NEP, social policy
3.1 The struggle for power 1924–28: Stalin's rivals and how he removed them
3.2 The use of terror in the 1930s: purges, NKVD, labour camps, show trials
3.3 Propaganda and censorship: socialist realism, education, religion, the 1936 Constitution
3.4 The Cult of Stalin: meaning, reasons and how it was achieved
4.1 Agriculture and collectivisation: kulaks, collective farms, the famine in Ukraine
4.2 Industry: Gosplan, the Five-Year Plans, Stakhanovites, successes and failures
4.3 Life in the Soviet Union: working and living conditions, experiences of different groups
4.4 The position of women and ethnic minorities: family, employment, persecution

topics.name: Option 31 Weimar and Nazi Germany, 1918–39
points: 1.1 The origins of the Republic 1918–19: the Kaiser's abdication, the armistice, the Weimar Constitution
1.2 Early challenges 1919–23: stab-in-the-back myth, Versailles, Spartacists, Kapp Putsch, the 1923 crises
1.3 The recovery of the Republic 1924–29: Stresemann, Rentenmark, Dawes and Young Plans, Locarno
1.4 Changes in society 1924–29: standard of living, position of women, cultural developments
2.1 Early development of the Nazi Party 1920–22: Hitler's early career, 25-Point Programme, the SA
2.2 The Munich Putsch and the lean years 1923–29: Mein Kampf, Bamberg Conference, limited support
2.3 The growth in support for the Nazis 1929–32: unemployment, fear of communism, Hitler's appeal, propaganda
2.4 How Hitler became Chancellor 1932–33: 1932 elections, Hindenburg, von Papen
3.1 Creation of a dictatorship 1933–34: Reichstag Fire, Enabling Act, Night of the Long Knives
3.2 The police state: Gestapo, SS, concentration camps, control of the legal system
3.3 Controlling and influencing attitudes: Goebbels, propaganda, media, sport, culture, the Churches
3.4 Opposition, resistance and conformity: support for the regime, the Churches, youth opposition
4.1 Nazi policies towards women: family, marriage, employment, appearance
4.2 Nazi policies towards the young: Hitler Youth, League of German Maidens, education
4.3 Employment and living standards: Labour Service, autobahns, rearmament, Labour Front
4.4 The persecution of minorities: racial beliefs, the Nuremberg Laws, Kristallnacht

topics.name: Option 32 Mao's China, 1945–76
points: 1.1 The Civil War 1945–49: strengths of the CCP and Guomindang, reasons for Mao's victory
1.2 Communist rule: Mao's ideology, his dominance, the CCP's role in government
1.3 Consolidating the CCP's hold 1951–52: terror, the 'three antis' and 'five antis' campaigns
1.4 The Hundred Flowers campaign 1956–57: reasons, features, the Anti-Rightist purge
2.1 Early changes in agriculture 1949–57: land redistribution, cooperatives, collectivisation
2.2 Industry and the First Five-Year Plan 1953–57: targets, Soviet help, results
2.3 The Great Leap Forward: communes, Lysenkoism, Lushan Conference, the Great Famine
2.4 Economic reform 1962–65: Liu Shaoqi, Deng Xiaoping and private farming
3.1 Reasons for the Cultural Revolution: power struggle and purifying communism
3.2 The Red Guards and the Red Terror: 1966 rallies, attacks on the 'four olds', destruction
3.3 The effects of the Cultural Revolution: political purges, social and economic impact
3.4 The end of the Cultural Revolution 1968–76: the PLA, return of Deng, the Gang of Four
4.1 Communist control: propaganda, the cult of Mao, Reform Through Labour camps
4.2 Family life and the role of women: Marriage Law 1950, end of foot binding
4.3 Education and health: literacy, Pinyin, barefoot doctors, collapse after 1966
4.4 Cultural change: attacks on traditional culture, religion and ancestor worship

topics.name: Option 33 The USA, 1954–75: conflict at home and abroad
points: 1.1 The position of Black Americans in the early 1950s: segregation, discrimination, voting rights, NAACP and CORE
1.2 Developments in education: Brown v. Topeka 1954 and Little Rock High School 1957
1.3 The Montgomery Bus Boycott and its impact 1955–60: Rosa Parks, Civil Rights Act 1957, King and the SCLC
1.4 Opposition to the civil rights movement: Ku Klux Klan, Emmett Till, Dixiecrats, White Citizens' Councils
2.1 Progress 1960–62: Greensboro sit-ins, Freedom Riders, James Meredith
2.2 Peaceful protests and their impact 1963–65: Birmingham and Washington, Freedom Summer, Civil Rights Act 1964, Selma, Voting Rights Act
2.3 Malcolm X and Black Power 1963–70: Stokely Carmichael, 1968 Olympics, Black Panthers
2.4 The civil rights movement 1965–75: riots and the Kerner Report, King's campaign in the North and assassination, progress by 1975
3.1 Reasons for US involvement 1954–63: domino theory, Diem, Kennedy, Strategic Hamlets
3.2 Escalation under Johnson: Vietcong threat, Gulf of Tonkin incident 1964
3.3 The nature of the conflict 1964–68: guerrilla tactics, Search and Destroy, Rolling Thunder, chemical weapons, Tet Offensive
3.4 Changes under Nixon 1969–73: Vietnamisation, Nixon Doctrine, Cambodia and Laos, bombing of North Vietnam
4.1 Opposition to the war: student movement, media, the draft, My Lai and Calley, Kent State
4.2 Support for the war: fear of communism, 'hard hats' and the 'silent majority'
4.3 The peace process and end of the war: Paris Peace Agreement 1973, economic and human costs
4.4 Reasons for the failure of the USA in Vietnam: North Vietnamese strengths, Ho Chi Minh Trail, US weaknesses, opposition at home
